episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for Monday, April 6, 2026. And here's who is innovating in higher education today.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends today, a University of Cincinnati College of Nursing study reveals a striking pattern in how students perceive A.I. assistance. According to the research, students rated chatbot responses highest for helpfulness and satisfaction when they did not know the source was artificial intelligence. Dr. Joshua Lambert, an associate professor and biostatistician, conducted a pilot project with seven Doctor of Nursing Practice students. Participants submitted statistical questions and received three blinded responses, one from a professor, one from a graduate assistant, and one from a custom A.I. chatbot. While blinded, students rated the chatbot responses highest. But when they identified or suspected A.I. as the source, those same answers received the lowest ratings. Lambert noted that students demonstrated a clear bias against A.I. responses once the source was revealed, even though they had preferred those exact responses moments earlier. The study, published in the Journal of Nursing Education, suggests deeper concerns about trusting A.I. in educational settings, even when the technology delivers quality answers.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Investing in Innovation, the University of Chicago received a fifty million dollar gift to reshape its approach to A.I. research and teaching. According to EdScoop, the donation from Rika and Joe Mansueto establishes the Mansueto Faculty of Mind and Machine Challenge, a matching initiative aiming to generate roughly two hundred million dollars total. The funds will recruit and support twenty scholars from diverse academic disciplines who exemplify computational thinking in their fields. University President Paul Alivisatos described the gift as advancing the institution during a signal period in intellectual history regarding A.I. and machine learning. The challenge builds on UChicago's existing A.I. Initiative, which currently supports ten faculty-led research projects and a dozen additional initiatives exploring computational approaches in education.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Turning to Case Study, Bridgewater State University in Massachusetts opened a Center for Artificial Intelligence last summer to help students gain skills needed across multiple industries. According to CBS News, graduate student Muhammed Yosef used A.I. tools through the center to build his portfolio and secured an internship at Metro South Chamber of Commerce, where he now develops chatbots to automate workflows. Political science senior Sam Oo worked as a Research and Innovation Assistant at the center, an experience that shifted his career perspective toward consulting. Eric LePage, assistant vice president for A.I. and ed tech innovation, noted that A.I. is being used across different fields and students need these skills to thrive. Dr. Anne Hird, a secondary education professor, emphasized that school administrators will soon look for A.I. skills in teachers.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Insights and Trends, the University of Florida AI² Summit drew nearly four hundred eighty educators, technologists, and academic leaders from one hundred twenty-nine institutions across thirty-nine states and ten countries. The summit, held March 29 to April 1 in Orlando, addressed foundational A.I. concepts, ethics, and classroom applications. NVIDIA co-founder Chris Malachowsky stated that anything that is a task is going to get automated, urging universities to shift focus toward critical thinking, judgment, and A.I. tool management. Troy Vingom, Kutztown University CIO, stressed the importance of teaching A.I. as an enabler across disciplines. Jesse Mendez, Kansas State University Provost, noted that A.I. technology changes every two weeks, making peer learning essential for institutional adaptation.

<break time="1.0s"/>

And in our second Case Study today, the University of Hawaii reports that fifty-one percent of students have engaged with campus A.I. chatbots since the start of the academic year, sending more than one hundred thousand text messages. UH Mānoa received over thirty-two thousand student messages through their chatbot, while UH West Oʻahu achieved a sixty-one percent engagement rate. Since January, the system completed more than three thousand automatic interventions connecting students with targeted resources, and nearly nineteen hundred students were flagged for staff follow-up. The chatbots saved staff approximately one hundred sixty-five hours. Kim Siegenthaler, senior advisor to the UH president, stated that this technology is helping shift from reactive to proactive support.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's today's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: UC Study Finds Students Prefer AI Chatbot Responses Until Source Revealed
leadStory.summary: According to a University of Cincinnati College of Nursing study, students rated AI chatbot responses highest for helpfulness and satisfaction when they did not know the source was artificial intelligence. Dr. Joshua Lambert, an associate professor and biostatistician, conducted a pilot project with seven Doctor of Nursing Practice students who submitted statistical questions and received three blinded responses from a professor, a graduate assistant, and a custom AI chatbot. Participants rated each response on helpfulness, satisfaction, and likelihood of use on a one-to-five scale. The chatbot responses received the highest satisfaction ratings while participants remained blinded. However, when students identified suspected AI responses, those same answers received the lowest ratings. Lambert noted that students preferred the large language model chatbot's responses when blinded yet demonstrated a bias against it when the source was suspected. He implemented the tool to lower barriers for students hesitant to ask professors questions on challenging topics. The study, co-authored by Robyn Stamm, Shannon White, Melanie Kroger-Jarvis of UC College of Nursing, and Bailey Martin of the University of Colorado, appeared in the Journal of Nursing Education.

The program will foster investments in research and education related to mind and machine topics, including efforts to expand machine learning and AI applications or deliberately limit their use in academic settings. University President Paul Alivisatos described the gift as advancing the institution during a signal period in intellectual history regarding AI and machine learning. quickHits.headline: AI² Summit Draws Nearly 480 Educators From 39 States
quickHits.summary: According to the University of Florida, the AI² Summit held March 29 to April 1, 2026 in Orlando drew nearly four hundred eighty educators, technologists, and academic leaders from one hundred twenty-nine institutions across thirty-nine states and ten countries. NVIDIA co-founder Chris Malachowsky stated that anything that is a task is going to get automated, urging universities to shift focus toward critical thinking, judgment, and AI tool management. Troy Vingom, Kutztown University CIO, highlighted faculty concerns about student learning and job displacement, stressing the importance of teaching AI as an enabler across disciplines. Jesse Mendez, Kansas State University Provost, noted that AI technology changes every two weeks, making peer learning essential for institutional adaptation. Director Hans van Oostrom said the broader participation demonstrated growing institutional demand. Malachowsky concluded that AI will become an underlying mechanism behind everything, urging institutions not to delay implementation.

quickHits.headline: University of Hawaii AI Chatbots Surpass 100,000 Student Messages
quickHits.summary: According to the University of Hawaii, fifty-one percent of UH students have engaged with campus chatbots since the start of the 2025-2026 academic year, sending more than one hundred thousand text messages. UH Mānoa received over thirty-two thousand student messages through their chatbot Bow, while UH West Oʻahu achieved a sixty-one percent student engagement rate with chatbot Pueo. Since January 2026, the chatbot system completed more than three thousand automatic interventions connecting students with targeted resources. Additionally, one thousand nine hundred twenty-four students were flagged for staff follow-up, and over nineteen hundred student questions were answered without human interaction. The AI chatbots saved staff approximately one hundred sixty-five hours. Kim Siegenthaler, senior advisor to the UH president, stated that this technology is helping shift from reactive to proactive support. At semester start, forty-seven percent of community college students felt good about the term while thirty-three percent felt nervous or overwhelmed.
